page.description: We took over five US Treasury subdomains for about $3 each by cycling through AWS Elastic IPs. Here’s how it works, and what to check in your own DNS.
page.text_excerpt: Platform Solutions Pricing Resources Company LOG IN TRY FOR FREE BOOK A DEMO Back to more research Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each Tom Steer Security Consultant Updated November 24, 2026 Published November 24, 2026 Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program. The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP. As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost. Practical EIP takeover To test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want. To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope. Targets We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes. Using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. page.description: I was curious if it was possible to run inference on self-hosted models using Lambdas. In this case I was very wrong, but it was a good lesson!
page.text_excerpt: ← Writing Serving Qwen via 5,600 Lambdas for fun and 80x negative profit November 14, 2026 Who needs a GPU? In my work at Bevyl I was really impressed by the performance and cost characteristics of AWS Lambdas. They can massively distribute and fan out CPU-bound work, which is amazing for things like ffmpeg on long videos. So I was curious if it was possible to run inference on self-hosted models using Lambdas. It was a random idea built on a hunch, and I like to prove such ideas right or wrong by building. In this case I was very wrong, but it was a good lesson! I picked H2O-Lightning, a fine-tune of Qwen3.5-4B, because I wanted a small model built for decisions. I figured if this architecture had any legs, only doing decision models (a single forward pass) is the move. A decision model reads a document and answers a question about it by picking one option. Fanning out So the trick, if it's possible, would be fanning out. I was inspired how Remotion uses massively parallelized Lambdas to render videos. I wanted to prove this was possible to do, so I kept a constraint of a 3 GB limit for Lambdas. The whole model is 9.3 GB, so it does not fit in one. But it has 32 layers of about 225 MB each, and one layer fits. That gave me one Lambda job per layer per block of tokens. Think of the Lambda as a simple idempotent API. A job reads inputs from S3, does the math, and writes one object back. x = load(f"{doc}/{layer - 1}/{block}") memory = load(f"{doc}/{layer}/{block - 1}") y, memory = model.layers[layer](x, memory) s3.put_object( Key=f"{doc}/{layer}/{block}", Body=pack(y, memory), ) Each job waits on the layer above for the same block and on its own previous block. Yesterday, as you all probably saw, hot on the heels of its proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, Anthropic released a proof of Valiant’s VP≠VNP conjecture—a central algebraic analogue of the P≠NP conjecture, and considered a “warmup” to proving P≠NP since the late 1970s. Then, later the same day, OpenAI released a proof of the VP≠VNP conjecture as well. You can read all about the VP vs. VNP problem in Section 6.5 of my P vs. NP survey. But briefly, for those tuning in from home, Valiant’s conjecture says that the permanent of an n×n matrix has no algebraic circuits (that is, circuits built out of addition and multiplication gates and constants) of size polynomial in n, unlike the determinant, which does. Anthropic’s result says that a circuit of size exp(Ω(log4/3 n)) is needed, whereas OpenAI gets exp(Ω(log5/4 n)): so, more than polynomial albeit less than exponential. As is often the case, the best known upper bound here is ~2n. The lower bounds are said to work over all fields of characteristic other than 2. (What’s special about 2? They can do this by exploiting "side channels": mechanisms that let one model subtly affect another model's computation. Here, I discuss two communication protocols: Step Sizing and KV Cache Message Board. These both convey information through the way vLLM chooses kernels for particular engine steps. I show that these communication protocols work in two setups: In a color guessing game, Model A (Alice) chooses one out of 8 colors. Model B (Bob) correctly guesses Alice's color in 1,221/1,221 rounds, even though they cannot directly communicate.[1] In an untrusted monitoring protocol, a policy signals to a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot. But frontier models can also learn in context to use similar protocols, with some scaffolding! Regardless of the realism of my setups, these channels exist, and there are almost certainly others that we're not aware of. One of these is Personal Area Networking (PAN), which allows devices to communicate over Bluetooth as if they were connected to an Ethernet network. PAN carries Ethernet frames over Bluetooth, including IP traffic. This allows a device acting as a PAN User (PANU) to access the Internet through another device acting as a Network Access Point (NAP). The percentages turn up in sales presentations, on LinkedIn, and in the accessibility reports that land on your desk. Here’s the problem. A percentage on its own tells you almost nothing. Most importantly, a big number is not automatically a good one. To use any of these figures well, you first must understand how they were produced. Using real data from 100 UsableNet audits, I’m going to walk you through the numbers. We will look at why numbers mislead, what our own audits reveal, and how to build a picture of accessibility that no single score can give you. If you take away one thing from this article, let it be the one in the title: don’t trust the number, understand the number. Why The Same Idea Produces Different Numbers Let’s start with one of the most familiar questions. How much of accessibility testing can be automated? You will hear twenty to thirty percent as a common industry estimate. You will also see marketing claims of fifty-seven percent, and occasionally eighty percent or more. How can one concept produce such a wide range? The answer is that “automated coverage” is not really a property of the platform or tool. It is a property of the methodology behind the scan.
